title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather — Korea's number-one small-talk topic — while adding two new tools: conditional -(으)면 and the guess -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요.
bekal: asking about and describing the weather
naming the four seasons and what happens in each
using the weather as an opening for small talk

dialogs.title: 대화 — A cloudy morning
dialogs.intro: Ani and Minjun meet at a bus stop. Notice that almost this whole conversation is weather small talk — and that this is completely normal in Korea.

notes: **The weather is Korea's number-one conversation opener** — not empty small talk, but a way to start talking without pushing. If you don't know what to say to a neighbor in the elevator, 날씨가 좋네요 is always right.
**비가 와요 uses 오다 (come), not 내리다 or 있다.** In Korean, rain and snow "come": 비가 와요, 눈이 와요. 비가 내려요 ("rain falls") is also correct but sounds more poetic and written. ⚠️ 비가 있어요 is not a sentence at all.

**-네요 expresses something you've just noticed.** 흐리네요 = "oh, it's cloudy, isn't it" — unlike 흐려요, which simply reports. This ending makes your sentences sound alive and invites a response, and Koreans use it constantly.

**맞아요 means "that's right" as agreement.** It's warmer than 네 and far more common for agreeing with someone's opinion. The alternatives are 아니에요, or 글쎄요 ("well, I'm not sure") when you doubt it but don't want to contradict.

**-는데 in 더웠는데 means "but" or "whereas", setting up a background.** It's one of the connectors Koreans use most and one of the hardest to explain — the full picture waits for B1. For now, just recognize that it prepares a gentle contrast.

**따뜻하게 means "warmly".** The ending **-게** turns an adjective into an adverb, like English "-ly": 따뜻하다 (warm) → 따뜻하게 (warmly), 맵다 (spicy) → 맵게 (spicily), 크다 (big) → 크게 (in a big way). Very productive and easy: 안 맵게 해 주세요 ("not spicy, please") uses it.

**-았으면 좋겠어요 means "I hope" or "I wish".** Literally "if it had happened, it would be good". It's the standard way to express a hope in Korean, and it makes no sense translated word for word. Learn it whole: 빨리 왔으면 좋겠어요, 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요.
**일년 내내 means "all year round".** 내내 means "throughout", and it attaches to a span of time: 하루 종일 (all day), 일주일 내내 (all week).

grammars.title: -(으)면 — if
body: Attach **-면** to vowel stems, **-으면** to consonant stems. Just like the -(으)ㄹ pattern you already know.
after: **The condition always comes first, the result after.** 비가 오면 택시를 탈 거예요 = if it rains, I'll take a taxi. English can flip the order ("I'll take a taxi if it rains"); Korean can't.
**Unlike -아서/어서, -(으)면 can be followed by commands and suggestions:** 시간이 있으면 오세요 (if you have time, come). That's one reason it's so useful for polite requests.
**-(으)면 is also used for habits:** 주말이 되면 늦게 일어나요 (on weekends, I get up late). Here it's closer to "whenever" than to "if".

grammars.title: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 — it seems
body: Expresses an uncertain guess. It uses the same -(으)ㄹ pattern, plus 것 같아요 ("it seems so").
after: **Koreans use this form far more often than foreign learners expect.** Stating an opinion directly (맛있어요! — it's delicious!) sounds blunter than is usually considered polite; softening it (맛있는 것 같아요 — I think it's delicious) is the standard way to share an opinion without imposing it.
⚠️ So don't translate 것 같아요 literally every time. Often it doesn't mean the speaker is unsure — just that they're being polite, like English "I think".
At A1, master the first form, **-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요**. Just recognize the rest.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: Be careful not to catch a cold.
Which season do you like best?

blocks.title: Korean winter if you're not used to cold
items: In January, Seoul often stays below zero all day, and the wind makes it feel much colder than the number says. If you grew up somewhere warm, this isn't just uncomfortable — it's exhausting.
Words you'll hear often: **내복** (thermal underwear), **핫팩** (disposable hand warmer) and **패딩** (thick down jacket). All three are sold everywhere and all three are worth the money.
⚠️ Indoors, Korea is actually very warm because the floors are heated (**온돌**). Layering is the answer: thick outside, thin underneath.
